issue_context.title: HttpTelemetry instrumentation for HTTP/3
issue_context.body:
Newly added `System.Net.Http` [Telemetry](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/HttpTelemetry.cs) should be expanded to HTTP/3 in the future. 

Currently, only the Start/Failed/Stop events are available for HTTP/3.
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/ncl
See info in area-owners.md if you want to be subscribed.

@ManickaP @CarnaViire Are there any major code changes planned for HTTP/3 during 7.0 that would be complicated if telemetry code were in place already?
I'm happy to do the change as long as it doesn't cause you more work in the long run.

No major changes planned. There might be some perf work around stream data handling, like: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/58445.
I don't think adding telemetry now will cause more work for us in the future. Feel free to tackle this and thanks for taking the initiative here!

review_comments: This is not exactly the moment when the headers get sent, but it gets muddy with the gathered buffer with content. How does this compare with H/2 and H/1.1? Is is worth trying to refine the moment or not?

On HTTP/2, we will actually include the time to write out the headers on the wire ([code](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/dc9979136cf0ff1addbc1a4c0f06ea4b65f002d4/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/Http2Connection.cs#L1529-L1587)). That is because the time when the headers are sent is well-defined since we immediately serialize the action on the multiplexed connection.

On HTTP/1.1 and 3, however, the headers may not end up being sent right away, but only with the first flush of the request content, which may be under user's control.
We could report a more accurate timestamp of when the headers are actually sent, but these events being Start/Stop complicates the matter. If ThreadPool activity tracking is on, I don't see how we would get the async scope for Start/Stop to match, given Stop would result as part of the content copying outside of `SendAsync`.
I guess this is good enough and not worth the trouble. Especially, if we're already not pedantic about the exact times in H/1.1

In case the connection gets closed in the meantime, the request will get retried on a different connection (line 224). I'm not sure what counts into the "waiting time in the queue" in such case, but this will report as request left the queue.

This should be rare-ish to happen, but yes, you may see multiple `RequestLeftQueue` events for a given request.

Similarly with 1.1, there is a race where we would retry if the server disconnects [here](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/dc9979136cf0ff1addbc1a4c0f06ea4b65f002d4/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L587-L593), logging `RequestLeftQueue` twice.
Similarly with resets on HTTP/2, we may re-insert the request to the queue.

I'm not sure we can/should improve that somehow. I feel it's still valuable to include the time on queue here even if the request will just end up back in the queue.

If we do similar thing with H/1.1 and H/2 then this is fine. I'm mostly trying to make sure we keep similar behavior between the protocols so that one counter doesn't mean something else based on HTTP version.
Why this change? Is it to unify exception types with H/2, H/1.1?

Right, this is something that both 1.1 and 2 seem to be doing.
E.g. for 1.1:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/dc9979136cf0ff1addbc1a4c0f06ea4b65f002d4/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L842

It seems harmless enough of a change (given TCE derives from OCE), or we could update the [failure tests](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/b3847f42ae95cc082a6b28575d4d847187b31a7b/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/tests/FunctionalTests/TelemetryTest.cs#L238) to expect OCE instead.
